passage:
At the park in Osaka, a smiling woman on a bench held out a pink sweet. "Want one?" Yuki, five, trotted toward her at once.
"Yuki, come back to me," called Aiko, his mother, catching his hand. "We don't take sweets from people we don't know." The woman nodded and put it away.
Later the wind blew Yuki's hat under a hedge. A tall park keeper in a grey coat, face serious, pulled it out and held it up. Yuki hid behind Aiko's legs.
"He works here, see his badge?" Aiko said softly. Yuki peeked, grabbed the hat and whispered, "Thank you."

qa.q: What did the woman on the bench hold out?
qa.a: A pink sweet.

qa.q: Why did Yuki trot toward the smiling woman but hide from the park keeper?
qa.a: The smile and the pink sweet felt nice, so she seemed safe, while the keeper's serious face made Yuki nervous, even though he was the one helping.

qa.q: What rule did Aiko use, and why does it suit a five-year-old?
qa.a: We don't take sweets from people we don't know; a simple rule protects Yuki when a nice feeling might make him trust too quickly.

qa.q: How might the park keeper feel when Yuki hides?
qa.a: He might feel a little sad, or be used to it, and glad when Yuki finally whispers thank you.

grounding: A five-year-old heads straight for a smiling stranger with a sweet but hides from a serious-looking park keeper who is helping him.

passage:
In the kindergarten garden, Vikas spotted shiny red berries on a hedge. "Sweets!" he said, and reached out.
"Stop, Vikas." Miss Fernandes knelt beside him. "Those aren't for eating. We only eat food from our tiffin or from grown-ups we know."
Near the gate, Deepak Bhaiya, the school caretaker with a big moustache and a mop, bent down. "Your lace is open, little one."
Vikas scrunched his face and ran back to Miss Fernandes, clutching her dupatta.
"That's Deepak Bhaiya. He helps us every day," she said. "Shall we let him tie it together?"
Vikas held her hand tight and stuck out one foot.

qa.q: What did Vikas spot on the hedge?
qa.a: Shiny red berries.

qa.q: Why did the berries seem good to Vikas but Deepak Bhaiya seem scary?
qa.a: The berries looked like sweets, so they felt nice and safe, while the big moustache and mop made him nervous, though Deepak Bhaiya only wanted to help.

qa.q: How did Miss Fernandes handle each of Vikas's feelings?
qa.a: She stopped the berries with a clear rule, and with the caretaker she named him and stayed close so Vikas could accept help while feeling safe.

qa.q: What might Deepak Bhaiya think when Vikas runs away?
qa.a: He may feel a little hurt, or be used to it, and patient enough to wait while the teacher introduces him.

grounding: A kindergarten child reaches for sweet-looking berries but runs from a kind caretaker, because nice and nervous feelings decide what seems safe.

I'm Irfan, and on Sunday I took my little brother Abhinav to the fair with Ammi.
A man in a sparkly hat was giving out free candyfloss near the back gate. Abhinav let go of my hand and ran straight to him. I caught up and pulled him back to Ammi.
Later he got lost for a minute near the swings. A lady at the help desk, in a plain brown sweater, knelt and asked his name. Abhinav screamed and wouldn't answer until Ammi came running.
I don't know exactly what he was thinking. Maybe sparkly felt friendly and plain felt scary. Now we practise who to ask for help.

qa.a: Free candyfloss.

qa.q: How did Irfan probably feel when Abhinav let go and ran?

Monday. "Drawing is the easiest thing in the world," Lokesh told his sister Lakshmi, colouring a kite. "And useful. Artists get rich." He shoved his maths book aside. "Fractions are impossible. Nobody ever uses them."
Wednesday. Lakshmi asked him to help cut paper for a real kite. "Half this side, a quarter there," she said. Lokesh folded and measured without a single complaint. He didn't notice it was fractions.
Saturday. In Sangeeta Ma'am's class, the fractions sheet came round. Lokesh groaned, "Pointless." Then he saw a question about sharing kite string and paused. "Wait, I did this with Didi."
He still said drawing was easier. But he finished the sheet.

qa.q: What did Lakshmi ask Lokesh to help with on Wednesday?
qa.a: Cutting paper for a real kite.

qa.q: Why does Lokesh think drawing is easy and fractions impossible?
qa.a: He loves drawing and dislikes maths, so his feelings supply the answer: what he enjoys feels simple and useful, what he dislikes feels hard and pointless.

qa.q: What did Lakshmi do that worked?
qa.a: She tied fractions to something he liked, cutting a kite, so he used them before his dislike could get in the way.

qa.q: How might Sangeeta Ma'am see Lokesh on Saturday?
qa.a: She would notice the usual groan, then a pause and a finished sheet, a small change she might want to build on.

grounding: Over several days, a boy calls his favourite subject easy and useful and a disliked one hard and pointless, until a kite shows the disliked one in use.

passage:
Ojas, your Nana has a confession. At eleven I adored geography. Maps, rivers, mountains. I told everyone it was the easiest subject and the only useful one, because one day I'd travel the world.
English, though? Pointless, I said. Too hard. I stared out of the window through every grammar lesson.
My teacher asked me once, "Harish, how will you ask for directions in all those countries?" I had no answer. I just didn't like English, so it felt useless.
Years later I did travel, for work. And what did I need every single day? Letters, forms, conversations. In English.
So when you tell me science is boring and pointless, I'll only ask: is it pointless, or do you just not like it yet?

qa.q: Which subject did Harish adore at eleven?
qa.a: Geography: maps, rivers, mountains.

qa.q: Why did English feel pointless to young Harish?
qa.a: He simply didn't like it, so it felt hard and useless, even though it mattered for the travel he dreamed about.

qa.q: What could Ojas do about science after hearing Nana's story?
qa.a: Ask whether science is really pointless or just not liked yet, and look for one way it connects to something Ojas enjoys.

qa.q: How might the teacher have felt when Harish had no answer?
qa.a: The teacher may have hoped the question would plant a seed, even if Harish kept staring out of the window.

grounding: A grandfather recalls how, as a boy, liking geography made it seem easy and useful while disliking English made it seem hard and pointless.

Only one hour before bedtime, and two tests tomorrow: science and Hindi. Pranav spread his science notes across the floor. "Science is easy," he told Himani Didi, who was minding him while his parents were at a wedding. "And useful. Hindi is hard and pointless."
"Which test is worth more marks?" Didi asked.
"Hindi," Pranav mumbled. "But I already know science."
The phone buzzed. It was Pallavi from his class. "Can you explain photosynthesis? You're so good at it."
Pranav beamed and talked for fifteen minutes.
When he hung up, the clock showed forty minutes left. Didi slid the Hindi book toward him. "Twenty minutes each?"
Pranav sighed, but opened it.

qa.q: Why does Pranav call Hindi hard and pointless?

qa.a: Asking which test was worth more and suggesting twenty minutes each, because it let the facts, not his feelings, guide his time.

qa.a: Pallavi sees him as the science expert to ask, which fits how much he likes science and probably makes him feel proud. 😊

"Chetan, it's just a small jump off the canal bridge. Everyone does it."
"The canal's got currents after the rain, yaar. And rocks."
"It's fine. It feels fine." Saurabh grinned, bouncing on his toes.
"Saurabh, you won't even do the swimming test at school. You said the deep end was dangerous."

"Then pass the swim test first. We'll find exciting things with a lifeguard around."

qa.a: The canal bridge.

qa.q: Why does the canal jump feel safe to Saurabh while the pool feels dangerous?
qa.a: The jump feels thrilling, so it seems low-risk; the smelly pool and shouting coach feel unpleasant, so they seem dangerous, though the facts point the other way.

qa.q: What question from Chetan helped, and what could Saurabh try next?
qa.a: Asking whether a lifeguarded pool is really more dangerous than a canal with rocks; next Saurabh could pass the swim test and look for thrills with safety around.

qa.a: Chetan is worried for his friend and has to be firm without sounding boring, so he offers a plan along with the warning.

passage:
Last year I'd have told you that riding pillion on my friend's scooter, no helmet, was nothing. The wind, the speed, the whole gang cheering: it felt amazing, so it felt safe.
But when Vasudha Ma'am announced the overnight science camp, I was the only boy in my group who refused. Strangers, tents, a forest. My stomach flipped just thinking about it, and I was sure it was dangerous.
It was my cousin Parul who made me write both down side by side, with facts. Scooter: no helmet, busy road, a fifteen-year-old driver. Camp: three teachers, a first-aid kit, a fenced campsite.
I stared at that list for a long time. The scary one was the safe one.
I went to the camp. I haven't got on that scooter since.
Vedant

qa.q: What safety facts did Vedant list for the camp?
qa.a: Three teachers, a first-aid kit, a fenced campsite.

qa.q: Why did the scooter ride feel safe to Vedant back then?
qa.a: The wind, speed and cheering felt amazing, and because it felt good, the risk seemed small.

qa.q: What did Parul's list do that feelings couldn't?
qa.a: It set the facts side by side, showing the thrilling ride was the risky one and the scary camp was the safe one.

qa.q: How might Vasudha Ma'am have felt when Vedant refused the camp?
qa.a: She might have been puzzled or disappointed, and glad later when he changed his mind.

grounding: A teenage boy looks back on judging an exciting helmetless ride as safe and a scary camp as dangerous, until listing facts reversed the picture.

passage:
Climbing club coach's note, Saturday. Shreya

Tushar, 15, arrived buzzing. He wanted to go straight to the overhang wall, no warm-up, no partner check. "It's easy, Coach, zero risk." He has fallen off that overhang twice this month.
Twenty minutes later Nazia, our assistant coach, set a slab route for him, our gentlest wall. He folded his arms. "That one's sketchy. I could slip." He finds slab climbing boring and awkward.
So the thrilling wall felt safe and the dull one felt dangerous. The facts point the other way.
What I did next: I asked him to rate each wall on a card, first by feel, then by the falls logged in our book. He went quiet at the second column. Then he did the warm-up and the partner check, and tried the slab.

qa.q: How many times has Tushar fallen off the overhang this month?
qa.a: Twice.

qa.q: Why does Tushar call the overhang 'zero risk'?
qa.a: It excites him, and that buzz makes it feel safe, even though his falls say otherwise.

qa.q: Why did Shreya's card exercise work?
qa.a: Rating each wall first by feel and then by the falls in the book let Tushar see for himself that his feelings and the facts disagreed.

qa.q: How might Nazia feel when Tushar calls her route sketchy?
qa.a: Nazia may feel her careful beginner route was judged unfairly, and may guess that his dislike, not the wall, is talking.

grounding: A coach records a teenage boy calling an exciting wall zero risk and a boring easy wall dangerous, and uses logged falls to check his feelings.

passage:
Mentor's log, Wednesday. Joseph

Reena brought me the supplier proposal for the new site today. Glossy, cheap, a charming sales call. She said, "Something about this makes me uneasy, and I can't say why yet. I don't want to sign on a feeling, and I don't want to ignore it either."
She'd made two columns on a notepad: what supports the unease, and what argues against it. Against: the price, and the samples looked fine. For: they wouldn't name past clients, and the delivery dates were vague.
She rang two firms in the same industrial park. One had used this supplier. Late deliveries, three months running.
What I did next: told her to write this up for the committee and keep the two columns in the report. That's a method worth copying.

qa.q: How many firms did Reena ring?
qa.a: Two firms in the same industrial park.

qa.q: What did Reena think her unease meant, and how did she treat it?
qa.a: She took it as a signal worth checking, not as proof, so she neither signed on a feeling nor brushed it aside.

qa.q: What made Reena's two-column method useful?
qa.a: It made her list evidence for and against her feeling, which led her to ring past clients and find the late deliveries.

qa.q: How does Joseph see Reena's approach?
qa.a: Joseph sees it as a method worth copying and wants the columns kept in the committee report.

grounding: A mentor records a young woman treating unease about a supplier as information and testing it with evidence before a big decision.

passage:
Tuesday night

The Chandigarh offer came today and my heart did a little dance. New city, bigger title, mountains on weekends. I wanted to reply YES before dinner.

Then I remembered what I promised myself after the last rushed move: feelings first, then facts, then decide.

Feeling: excited, with a tiny knot of worry underneath.
Facts for: a better role, and a team lead who answered all my questions honestly.
Facts against: rent there is higher, and the raise barely covers it. And the knot? It's Nirmala Aunty, my landlady here, who has called me "beti" and sent up parathas since the day I moved in.

So the excitement is real, and so is the knot. Tomorrow I'll ask about a better salary and call two people who work there. Then I'll decide.
Gurpreet

qa.q: What does Nirmala Aunty send up?
qa.a: Parathas.

qa.q: What does the 'tiny knot of worry' tell Gurpreet?
qa.a: It points to real facts, the higher rent and leaving Nirmala Aunty, so the excitement isn't the whole picture.

qa.q: What steps is Gurpreet taking before deciding?
qa.a: Asking about a better salary and calling two people who work there, so the choice rests on facts as well as feelings.

qa.q: How might Nirmala Aunty feel if Gurpreet moves?
qa.a: She would probably miss her a lot, while still being glad for her new role. 🤍

grounding: A young woman notes her excitement and worry about a job offer, treats both as information, and checks the facts before deciding.

Class 4 observation note, Friday. Charu, maths teacher

I put the puzzle on the board: A bat and a ball cost 110 rupees together. The bat costs 100 rupees more than the ball. How much is the ball?
Lavanya's hand shot up. "Ten!" Half the class nodded.
I only said, "Check it before I do." Lavanya frowned, whispering. "Ball ten, then bat is one hundred and ten, together that's one hundred and twenty. Oh!" She tried again with her pencil. "Five! Ball five, bat one hundred and five."
Afterwards she told me, "The first answer felt so right that I didn't check it."
What I did next: we made a class signal, a finger on the lips, for 'pause before you shout'. Lavanya asked to be the one who reminds everyone.

qa.q: What was Lavanya's first answer?
qa.a: Ten.

qa.q: Why did 'ten' feel right to Lavanya?
qa.a: The numbers 110 and 100 made ten pop out instantly, and because it came so easily it felt correct without checking.

qa.q: What class habit did Charu start, and how does it help?
qa.a: A finger on the lips to mean pause before you shout, which gives the slow check a chance to catch quick wrong answers.

qa.q: How might the classmates who nodded at 'ten' feel after Lavanya's correction?
qa.a: Surprised and a bit sheepish, and perhaps more willing to check their own quick answers next time.

grounding: A teacher records a child catching her own quick wrong answer to a trick puzzle by pausing to check it.

At the small shop by the bus stand, Dilnaz Khala was weighing onions when Zeenat came in for matchboxes.
"Riddle for you," Khala said, eyes twinkling. "Which is heavier, a kilo of cotton or a kilo of iron?"
"Iron!" Zeenat said, then stopped, because Khala's eyebrows had gone up.
Zeenat looked at the scale: onions on one side, the brass weight on the other. She tapped the weight. "A kilo is a kilo," she said slowly. "Cotton would just be bigger. They're the same!"
"Why did you say iron first?"
"Iron feels heavy. My mouth answered before my head."
Khala laughed and slipped a toffee in with the matchboxes. On the walk home, Zeenat tried the riddle on two cousins. Both said iron.

qa.q: What did Zeenat come to the shop to buy?
qa.a: Matchboxes.

qa.q: Why did 'iron' feel like the right answer at first?
qa.a: Iron feels heavy, so the quick answer jumped out before Zeenat thought about what a kilo means.

qa.q: What helped Zeenat catch the mistake?
qa.a: Pausing when she saw Khala's raised eyebrows, looking at the brass weight on the scale, and reasoning it through.

qa.q: What might Dilnaz Khala enjoy about asking riddles?
qa.a: She enjoys the moment children stop and think, and the toffee rewards Zeenat for catching her own mistake. 🙂

grounding: A child in a small-town shop blurts the wrong answer to a trick question, then pauses and reasons her way to the right one.

passage:
At home, Deepak spent a whole week choosing a second-hand cycle. He tested the brakes on three, asked the mechanic in the bazaar about spare parts, and kept a list in his notebook. His sister Mahima teased him about it.
Then came the temple fair. With four friends crowding round the ring-toss stall, the stall owner shouted, "Last chance, big prize!" Somebody said, "Deepak won't dare."
Deepak slapped down all his fair money. Ten throws, ten misses. The friends howled; he laughed along, cheeks burning.
On the walk back, alone with Mahima, he went quiet. "If I'd been by myself, I'd have counted how many rings actually land. I watched nobody win all evening."
"So why didn't you?"
"They were watching," he said, and kicked a stone.

qa.q: How many cycles did Deepak test the brakes on?
qa.a: Three.

qa.q: Why did Deepak slap down all his fair money at the stall?
qa.a: With friends watching and a dare in the air, excitement and pride took over, pushing him into a snap choice he'd never make alone.

qa.q: What could Deepak try the next time friends egg him on?
qa.a: Set a spending limit before going out, or say 'give me a minute' and step aside to think, the way he did with the cycle.

qa.q: How does Mahima see her brother that evening?
qa.a: She has seen the careful, list-making Deepak and now the impulsive one, so she asks why, curious rather than mocking.

grounding: A teenager chooses a cycle carefully alone but blows his money on a dare at a fair with friends watching.

passage:
On Sunday afternoons in Johannesburg, Alejandro practised quiz questions at the kitchen table, slow and careful, crossing out wrong guesses. He got nearly all of them right.
Friday's inter-school final was different. The hall was packed, his friends were chanting his name, and the buzzer felt hot under his palm. The host read, "How many months have twenty-eight days?" Alejandro slammed the buzzer. "One! February!"
"Incorrect."
Zanele, his teammate, buzzed after a pause. "All twelve."
Alejandro stared at the desk. At home, he'd have seen that in a second.
At the break Zanele said, "You're brilliant at the kitchen table. Out here you're racing the crowd."
In the second half he kept his hand flat on the desk for one slow breath before each buzz. They lost by two points, but he didn't miss another.

qa.q: What did Alejandro answer to the months question?
qa.a: One, February.

qa.q: Why did Alejandro buzz before thinking in the final?
qa.a: The packed hall, his chanting friends and the hot buzzer made him feel rushed and excited, which pushed him into the fast, gut mode.

qa.q: What change did Alejandro make in the second half, and why did it help?
qa.a: He kept his hand flat for one slow breath before each buzz, giving the careful thinking he uses at home time to catch up.

qa.q: How does Zanele see Alejandro's mistake?
qa.a: Zanele sees a brilliant thinker racing the crowd, not a careless one, and says so kindly at the break.

grounding: A teenager reasons carefully at home but snaps out wrong answers in front of a cheering crowd, then adds a breath to slow down.

In the school corridor, the elective forms were due by Friday. Zeenat and three others crowded round Tanuja's locker.
"We're all doing computer science. You're in, right?"
"Obviously," Tanuja said, and scribbled it on the form right there, pen pressed against the locker door. Everyone cheered.
That evening in the empty library, she read the form again, calmer. Biology was her best subject. She wanted to be a vet. And computer science clashed with the biology lab slot.
Next morning she went to the careers room. The counsellor asked, "What did you choose, and when?" Tanuja laughed. "In ten seconds, with an audience."
She rewrote the form: biology. At lunch she told Zeenat, who shrugged. "Fair. We'll still sit together."

qa.q: Where did Tanuja first fill in the elective form?
qa.a: In the school corridor, pressed against the locker door.

qa.q: Why did Tanuja say 'Obviously' so quickly?
qa.a: With friends crowding round and cheering, belonging felt more important in that moment than thinking through her own plans.

qa.q: What helped Tanuja choose well the second time?
qa.a: Rereading the form alone in the calm library, weighing her marks, her goal and the timetable clash, then talking to the counsellor.

qa.q: How does Zeenat react to Tanuja's change of mind?
qa.a: Zeenat calls it fair and says they'll still sit together, showing the friendship never depended on the same subject.

grounding: A teenager snaps a subject choice with friends watching, then reasons it through calmly alone and changes it.

passage:
Ivan chose lunch in Lisbon the way he always did: two seconds at the café counter, "the soup, please," done. Same with which tram to catch or what to wear to class. Familiar ground, small stakes; the gut was fine.
The two-year lease on the flat above the bakery was another matter. The landlord wanted a signature by the weekend, and the flat was bright and lovely. Ivan felt the pull.
Instead he printed a checklist: rent against his part-time wages, the notice period, the damp patch in the bathroom. He slept on it twice. On Saturday he showed it to Beatriz, a friend who had rented for years.
"Ask them to fix the damp in writing," she said. "And check the break clause."
Ivan did both before signing on Monday.

qa.q: What did Ivan order at the café counter?
qa.a: The soup.

qa.q: Why was Ivan happy to decide lunch in two seconds but not the lease?
qa.a: Lunch is familiar and small, so his gut is good enough; a two-year lease is big and hard to undo, so the pull of the bright flat needed checking.

qa.q: Which tools did Ivan use for the big decision?
qa.a: A printed checklist, sleeping on it twice, and advice from Beatriz, who had rented for years.

qa.q: How might the landlord see Ivan's requests?
qa.a: The landlord might find them a little fussy, but would likely see a careful tenant who will be reliable.

grounding: A young man decides everyday things by gut but uses a checklist, sleep and a friend's advice for a two-year lease.

In the university mess, Rehana picked her tray in the time it took to say "rajma rice". Same with her seat in lectures or her library corner. Small, familiar choices; no need to agonise.

Zainab read the list. "Is it design you want, or getting away from one bad week?"
Rehana thought. "Both, maybe. Can I sit in on a design class first?"
Zainab signed a visitor pass.

qa.q: What did Rehana want to do after the bad week in the coding lab?
qa.a: Fill in the transfer form that same afternoon.

qa.q: What was Rehana feeling unsure about when Zainab asked her question?
qa.a: Whether she truly wanted design or mainly wanted to escape one bad week; she admits it might be both.

qa.q: Why did Rehana's slow approach suit this choice?
qa.a: A course switch is big and costly to undo, so a checklist, a week of sleep, advice and a trial class fit better than the quick gut she uses for lunch.

qa.q: How might Zainab view Rehana's checklist?
qa.a: Zainab probably sees a student taking a big decision seriously, which makes it easy to help with one sharp question.

grounding: A student trusts quick instinct for mess and seating choices but slows down with a checklist, sleep and advice before switching courses.

Dear Lakshmi Mashi,

You told me at the wedding to trust my gut, and I've been thinking about when that works.

For small things it's perfect. I pick my train compartment, my lunch, which assignment to do first, all by feel, and I'm usually right because I've done them a hundred times.

But the scholarship offer from Hyderabad isn't small. It means leaving Kolkata, a new language, and a bond to teach for two years afterwards. My gut screamed yes the second I read it.

So I did it the slow way. A checklist of what I'd gain and lose. Three nights' sleep. A call with a senior who took the same scholarship last year.

The answer is still yes, but now I know why, and I know about the bond.

Love,
Bidisha

qa.q: How many nights did Bidisha sleep on the scholarship decision?
qa.a: Three nights.

qa.q: Why does Bidisha trust gut feeling for lunch and train compartments?
qa.a: Bidisha has done them a hundred times, so quick feelings are usually right and little is lost if they're not.

qa.q: What did the slow way add, even though the answer stayed yes?
qa.a: It brought the two-year teaching bond into view and gave clear reasons, so the choice is made knowingly, not on excitement alone.

qa.q: How might Lakshmi Mashi feel reading this letter?
qa.a: Lakshmi Mashi might feel proud that the advice was taken thoughtfully, and reassured that such a big step was checked. 😊

grounding: A student explains using gut feeling for routine choices and a checklist, sleep and a senior's advice for a big scholarship decision.

Gurleen, you asked how to handle your two new team members. Let me tell you about Sudha and Firoz from my years at the pump factory, where everyone called me Kishore Sir.
Sudha would spend a whole morning deciding whether to order blue or black pens. Checked three suppliers. For pens!
Firoz was the opposite. When we had to choose a new machine for the assembly line, a huge purchase, he picked one because the salesman had worked with his cousin. "I just know," he said.
I made a mistake at first. I told Sudha to be faster about everything, and Firoz to be slower about everything. Neither listened.
What finally worked was simpler. I'd ask: how big is this, and can we undo it? Pens, small, undoable: five minutes. A machine: a week, a checklist, three opinions.
Size the effort to the decision, beta.

qa.q: What did Sudha spend a whole morning deciding?
qa.a: Whether to order blue or black pens.

qa.q: Why did Firoz feel so sure about the machine?
qa.a: The salesman had worked with his cousin, so the machine felt trustworthy, and that warm feeling replaced the checking a huge purchase needs.

qa.q: What question did Kishore end up asking, and how could Gurleen use it?
qa.a: How big is this, and can we undo it? Gurleen can ask the new team the same thing to decide how much time each choice deserves.

qa.q: How might Sudha and Firoz have felt when told to change everything?
qa.a: Both probably felt their whole style was being criticised, which is why neither listened until the advice fit the size of each decision.

grounding: A retired senior recalls watching one colleague over-analyse pens and another gut-pick a costly machine, and learning to match effort to each decision.

qa.q: What did Pradeep do well under time pressure?
qa.a: Pradeep settled the trivial plate question in seconds and slowed down only the big move, asking for capacity, parking and exits to be checked.

qa.q: How might Roshni feel after the call back?
qa.a: Roshni might feel a jolt at how close the gut choice came to going wrong, and be glad the check happened before the announcement.

grounding: Under time pressure, a coordinator notices one colleague over-thinking plates and another gut-deciding a venue move, and helps each match effort to stakes.
